newsitem.title: USA: Manufacturing index shows strength; markets tumble.
newsitem.headline: Manufacturing index shows strength; markets tumble.

text.p: Economic growth accelerated in December, a survey of purchasing managers showed Thursday, spooking financial markets and sending stock and bond prices skidding.

The National Association of Purchasing Management said its manufacturing index jumped to 54.0 in December, the highest in six months, from 52.7 in November. A reading above 50 shows an expanding manufacturing sector, while one below that level indicates contraction.

"The manufacturing sector grew more rapidly in December than in November with new orders indicating faster rates of growth and prices moving upward," Norbert Ore, who heads the group's monthly survey, said in a statement.

The report, the first broad glimpse of the economy each month, was also the first major indicator of the new year and had been widely awaited in financial markets. Private economists had expected a reading of 51.5 for December.

"Overall, it's a healthy number and compared to expectations it's a surprise," said Raymond Worseck, chief economist at A.G. Edwards & Sons Inc. "The economy has a reasonable rate of momentum going into 1997."
The survey data followed Tuesday's reports on robust new home sales in November and a jump in consumer confidence in December, news that also hit financial markets.

The purchasing group said its index of prices paid rose to 51.5 last month from 45.9 in November, indicating rising prices after two months of declines. It was the highest reading since July 1995, when the index was 59.
So far, most price increases have been absorbed by manufacturers and retailers and not passed on, helping to keep a lid on consumer price inflation.
But bond market investors, keenly sensitive to any signs of possible inflation, sent prices tumbling after the report. Inflation erodes the returns on their long-term investments.

The drop in bonds helped drive stocks lower, and the Dow Jones industrial average was down mroe than 60 points at 6,387 in early afternoon trading after falling as much as 95 points earlier. Stock investors were also nervous after Tuesday's slide of 101 points in the 30-share industrial average.
The 30-year Treasury bond fell 1-9/32, or $12.81 on a $1,000 bond, raising its yield to 6.75 percent from 6.64 percent on Tuesday. Bond prices and yields move in the opposite direction.
But some economists suggested that financial markets may have overreacted to the news.

"We're getting signs that growth is moderate and if anything a tad stronger," said Nicholas Perna, chief economist at Fleet Financial Group. "I think the market reaction to these numbers is exaggerated."

In its report, the purchasing group said 13 percent of purchasing managers reported paying higher prices in December, 13 percent reported paying lower prices and 74 percent said prices were unchanged from November.
The group's members buy goods ranging from cardboard to computer chips and other finished and raw materials for the nation's major corporations.
The purchasing survey especially rattled bond traders, who noted that the index has neared levels that historically have presaged Federal Reserve credit tightenings.

But one economist maintained that gyrations in the markets could have the same effect as a Fed tightening if continued sell-offs ultimately hamper economic growth by making it difficult, for example, for companies to raise the equity capital they need to expand.

"My concern is that wobbles in the financial markets could feed back to the economy," said Irwin Kellner, chief economist at Chase Manhattan's regional bank. "While I'm forecasting another year of economic growth, I do it with my fingers crossed."
Economists noted that the markets largely ignored another report pointing to weakness in labour markets.
The Labour Department said the number of Americans filing new claims for unemployment benefits climbed last week to the highest level since mid-July.
But in another measure of labour activity, the Conference Board said its help-wanted advertising index rose three points to 85.0 in November.
In the last three months, the volume of help-wanted advertising increased in eight of the nine U.S. regions.
